name: Rashi Agrawal
bio:
Rashi Agrawal is the Head of Agentic AI at Hinge Health, where she engineers high-stakes, secure, and HIPAA-compliant systems. Operating at the pioneer edge of generative AI technology, she architects state-of-the-art frameworks that move beyond simple automation to solve critical problems and drive dramatic business growth.

Previously, as Head of AI at Goodleap, a leading FinTech in Green Energy, Rashi spearheaded enterprise-wide transformation initiatives that optimized complex loan processing and customer engagement. Blending holistic vision with deep technical expertise, she successfully deployed intelligent decision-making and risk assessment platforms that delivered measurable value.

Earlier in her career, Rashi led engineering teams at Yahoo, maturing early-stage technical challenges into massive growth engines for their multi-billion-dollar Advertising business. Her leadership ensures innovation is grounded in business strategy, establishing AI as a competitive moat rather than just an operational layer.

Beyond the office, Rashi is a global explorer who has traveled to over 50 countries. A prominent thought leader in the engineering community, she is an Indian immigrant with a Master’s in Software Engineering from San Jose State University, an alumna of the Stanford Graduate School of Business Executive Education program, and the founder of Women In Tech AI (WIT AI), an organization dedicated to empowering and elevating women leaders in the field.

talks.title: Guardrails First: Engineering Member-Facing Health AI

sessions.scheduled_title: Guardrails First: Engineering Member-Facing Health AI

quotes.quote: We do have a lot of frontier models which are running and believe it or not, 40 million people actually use these models for triaging their health care issues.
The first independent safety test of a consumer health AI out of Mount Sinai found that this health AI is under triaging life-threatening emergency 50% of the times.
In February, ECRI the patient safety group that hospitals trust to rank their top risks named AI chatbot misuse as the number one health technology hazard of 2026.
Most AI safety failures in health care are not model failures. They are architectural decisions that were made before even a single token was generated.
Two, deterministic rules belong above the model, not inside it. What can never be wrong cannot be left to probability.
Launch of your product is where the real risk starts, not where it ends.
The architecture version strips PHI at the pipeline boundary. At ingestion before it ever reaches the data lake. By the time the data is stored, the PHI is gone.
You cannot slap on HIPAA on top of, you know, an underlying system or an architecture. You start with it and let the architecture grow around it.
A model is not a guardrail. A model with a system prompt is also not a guardrail. Code that runs above the model is closer.
If the labs themselves don't trust the prompt as a security boundary, neither should you.
If a member mentions self-harm, suicidal ideation, or an acute medical emergency, the system must route to 911 or 988. The model should not even see this turn.
Anything that touches member data has to check that the right member is at the other end. That's an authentication check. And authentication is a security bound boundary. Prompts are not.
What actually holds up in production is judges that continuously keep scoring real conversations as they happen. Not a saved golden data set. Live traffic.
The bottleneck is not the compute, the models, the capability. It's actually having enough people to read the signal and act on it.
A new failure that you see in production simply means you now have a new judge.
A bug that lightly annoys 100% of users is way less severe than one that could cause serious harm in 0.1% of cases.
You never quietly downgrade a bug just because you can't get to it.
Shipping a real safety bug is much worse than delaying for a false alarm.
Your launch bar is what your org already accepts in production, not what it says it will accept.
Fast follows are committed debt, not an optional backlog.
In a non-deterministic system, the judge is also non-deterministic. Before you trust the score, verify the scorer.
The rule is always ask, is the judge right before changing the agent's response? Fixing a judge prompt is not cheating. Judges are software, too.
Don't policy what you can architect. Don't prompt what you can code. Don't gate what you can monitor.
We are not building a generic low-stakes chatbot. We are building a system that has to be worthy of someone's health.

positions.claim: Most AI safety failures in healthcare are architectural decisions made before generation, not model failures.
Consumer health AI under-triages life-threatening emergencies 50% of the time, per the first independent safety test out of Mount Sinai.
ECRI named AI chatbot misuse the number one health technology hazard of 2026.
PHI should be stripped at ingestion, at the pipeline boundary, rather than redacted at runtime when logs or dashboards are written.
Production and non-production environments must have no data pipes between them, because a single pipe is enough to leak member data into dev.
Engineers outside the certified geographic region should have no access to raw PHI at all.
A system prompt is not a guardrail, because every authority layer above user is one prompt injection away from being overridden.
Emergency escalation, high-stakes intent routing, and identity verification must be handled by deterministic code that runs before the model on every turn.
Pre-launch eval checklists on saved golden datasets are necessary but insufficient; continuous scoring of live traffic is what holds up in production.
Per-message thumbs up/down member feedback is the truth signal and catches tone problems that automated judges miss.
High-stakes cases should be sampled and human-reviewed 100% of the time, with random sampling across other capabilities.
The scaling bottleneck for safe AI is human capacity to read and act on signal, not compute or model capability.
Some failure classes cannot be prompted away — each fix buys less, and the failure rate never reaches zero.
Severity must be set by the worst plausible outcome rather than by frequency or average impact.
A bug's severity is independent of who owns it, whether the team has capacity, and how hard the fix is; the only options are fix, delay, or accept with explicit sign-off.
Under uncertainty, hold and fix safety bugs but ship polish bugs, because the cost asymmetry runs in opposite directions.
A behavior already live in production for weeks or months without escalation or complaints cannot be called a launch blocker for a new feature.
Fast follows are committed debt rather than optional backlog items.
When a judge score drops, the first action should be verifying the judge, not changing the agent's prompts.
Editing a judge prompt is legitimate engineering, not gaming the eval, because judges are software that must evolve.
Building guardrails first is slower than bolting them on later, and that cost is an accepted design tradeoff for health-stakes products.
The bar for safety architecture should scale with stakes — generic low-stakes chatbots do not need this apparatus.
